en: Directing the Dead toward a Happy Rebirth by Śūnyatāsamādhivajra [Oxford,
Summer Vacation 2008, input by Péter-Dániel Szántó]
\A = Palm-leaf Tokyo composite manuscript (no title given), new no. 307, old no. 306; dated *samvat* 589 [= 1469 CE], written in Hook-topped Newari script.
\B = Kaiser Library 494 = NGMPP C 47/9 (not collated here); written in Bhujimol script, earlier than \A.
For further information on this text, see Tanemura 2007, *NGMCP Newsletter*; he also announced there a future edition.
There are two Tibetan translations of this work: Tōh. 1908, vol. phi, 35r1–38r6, and Tōh. 1907, vol. phi, 31v4–35r1.
It consists primarily of Āryā verses. Synopsis:

The first part (vv. 1–34) constitutes the yoga of reviving the dead (*mṛtasañjīvana-yoga*), based on a method taught in chapter 14 of the *Guhyasamāja*. The officiant reinstates the consciousness (*jñāna*) of an individual into his corpse, bestows initiation upon him, and guides it to exit through the crown of the head. Note the parallels with the *Catuṣpīṭha* regarding the apertures.

He becomes liberated or proceeds to a buddhakṣetra. Furthermore, one should note the parallels with Śaiva traditions regarding *parokṣadīkṣā* and *śāṅkarī dīkṣā*. [Please verify these terms, as I may not recall them correctly.]

The second part (vv. 34–85) is the rite for preventing the deceased from falling into the lower realms, performed during and after cremation. The scriptural authority for this is the *Sarvadurgatipariśodhana-tantra*. In this rite, the *ācārya* strikes and washes the bones and the garments to remove various obstacles.
Ryūgen notes that almost the entire text has been incorporated into Darpaṇācārya’s *Ācāryakriyāsamuccaya* within the section on the *antyeṣṭi* (funeral rites) for a *vajrācārya*.
Text of manuscript \A [1v]: *Oṃ namo locanāyai* ||
Having prostrated before the goddess named Locanā, the reviver of the dead, who is most intent on the welfare of others.
I shall now describe the application for the bestowal of a good rebirth upon the deceased through the *mṛtasaṃjīvanī* (life-restoring) yoga.

[1] In a well-secluded house of the deceased, the yogi, provided with all ritual offerings, wearing a white flowered turban (*uṣṇīṣa*), anointed with white perfumes, and being tranquil, [should practice]. [2]
Clad in white garments and ornaments, having resolved upon his former abode or another,
and holding a vajra and a vajra-bell, he should stand upon a high,
soft seat. Before him, with white sandalwood and other perfumes mixed with the water of the five nectars...
Having smeared the mandala, one should adorn it with white flowers.
[4*] Beginning with "adya" (today) and so forth, one should accumulate [the offerings] with one's own mantras ending in "svāhā," accompanied by exhortations.
Having visualized one's own seed-syllable on the moon at the heart, one should protect the site and so forth. [5*]
In that regard, the mantra to be protected through the yoga of one's own place is:
*oṃ āḥ vighnāntakṛt hūṃ*;
or alternatively, *oṃ namaḥ samanta...* and so forth.
Having duly performed the union with Locanā according to the ritual rules, the yogin, who knows the ordinances,
should cause the well-accomplished solar disc to emerge from the seed-syllable of the heart.
By means of that, he should bring forth the intensely red gnosis (jñāna), which is his own life-force (svadhā) residing in the other world.
Or else, having assumed the form of the entrance to the Dharma, like a steady lamp,

one should bring that knowledge and cause it to enter the heart of the deceased with the head. Having caused it to enter, one should behold him, arisen from that state, endowed with primordial wisdom (jñāna).

Then, having cast the syllable *moharati* into the heart, one should incinerate it with a garland of its rays; having emptied that body, one should dissolve it until only consciousness remains. Thereafter, reciting the syllable *moharati*, one should meditate upon that [consciousness] in the form of Locanā.
One should cause that eye and so forth, as well as the body and so forth, to remain entirely stable.
Having placed this heart-knowledge (hṛdayajñāna) upon the moon in the heart of the deity with the root mantras, one should [proceed].
Sprinkling with nectars from the clouds of the goddesses, sharpened by the essence of light;
because the entire circle of the sky was pervaded by those [nectars] emitted from his own body,
he should sprinkle [the disciple] with clouds of tears that appear as masses of rays.
One should sprinkle [the disciple] according to the rule with water filled with the recitation of that mantra;
and one should place a crown upon the head and a vajra and vajra-bell in the pair of hands.
Thereafter, having visualized the tip of a blade of kuśa grass as a sharp, single-pointed vajra by means of mantras...

Having cast it into the vajra-aperture, one should meditate upon it as resembling a blazing fire. Thereafter, with a concentrated mind, one should impel that flickering gnosis placed within the heart by means of flaming vajra-fires raised up by the wind.
One should meditate on it as rising up, being touched by fire like mercury,
or as the pure Buddha-field liberated from the upper self.
If, however, through conceptualization, one falls into the ocean of saṃsāra according to one's own ignorance.

Therefore, one should effect its departure by way of the upward path. By means of the head, it should go to the formless realm (*ārūpya*); by means of the *ūrṇā*-hair, it should go to that which is called the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).

Through the two eyes, one attains human status; through the two ears, the state of a Siddha or a deity; through the two nostrils, the state of a Yakṣa; and through the mouth, one may emerge as a Gandharva. [21*] The realm known as the Form Realm (rūpadhātu) [is attained].
Through the navel one goes to the state of desire or immortality; through the path of the semen, to the destination of the departed spirits (pretas).
Through the path of urine, one goes to the womb of lower animals; through the anus, to the state of hell.
While passing, one should avoid these paths.

Then, for the purpose of establishing him in the city of liberation, the Vajrācārya—who has been authorized by all the preceptors through the ritual of the *yājava*—should perform the *śāntika* homa in the fire of gnosis (*jñānāgni*) according to the procedure taught for a single-substance homa or by the prescribed rule. At that time, he should cause [the candidate] to recite Mahāyāna sūtras such as the *Prajñāpāramitā*, ten thousand times.

Thereafter, having withdrawn everything up to the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), the one who provided the sacrificial fee (*yojanaka*) should also respectfully give to the preceptor (*ācārya*) a sacrificial fee consisting of garments, ornaments, beds, seats, houses, fields, female slaves, male slaves, and so forth, in accordance with his own wealth.
Then, after reciting the mantras to be chanted over their hearts, he should cause the persons who performed the funeral rites to put on sacred threads (*yajñopavīta*).

Having visualized Kāla and Kapāla as the bearers of the corpse; Devarāja as the holder of the parasol; Brahmā as the wielder of the fly-whisk; Viṣṇu as the bearer of the sword; Śaṅkara as the reciter of praises; Yama as the performer of the funeral rites; Varuṇa as the bearer of the water-pot; Vahni as the bearer of the sacrificial ladle and spoon; Nairṛti as the bearer of food and drink; Vāyu as the bearer of the banner; and all the minor gods, asuras, and so forth—having thus visualized them.
Then, having recited the hundred-syllable mantra seven times and having properly dedicated his own merit toward perfect enlightenment, he should rise.

Having risen, the Vajrācārya, whose nature is that of the Vajradhara, the progenitor of all Buddhas, should proceed in front while reciting the Locanā mantra and all the mantras for the purification of miserable rebirths as taught in the *Durgatipariśodhana-tantra*. And on the path, he should be escorted and led by the World-Protectors (Lokapālas). He is thus brought forward, having ceased [all worldly activity].
One should behold him being incessantly praised by the gods and Agni,
and worshipped with the sounds of various musical instruments, auspicious songs, and the chanting of the *Aśanigīta*, accompanied by the resonances of bells, kettledrums, flutes, and lutes.
Equipped with the fivefold offerings, worship, canopies, curtains, banners, and parasols,

one should cause [the deceased] to reach the abode of the ancestors, which is well-supplied with many provisions, by means of dogs. There, having constructed two auspicious funeral pyres with dry fuel of milk-trees, [one should perform the rites].
There, one should pour water from a vessel over the heap of bones.
Then, with ritual worship, one should kindle it with fire until that heir becomes completely reduced to ashes, being well-composed.
As before, one should cause the Sūtra of the Great Rise of the Mahāyāna to be recited, and one should have the Vajra-song sung, accompanied by cymbals and the ḍamaru drum. O ||

Now, some people, though following the path to liberation, proceed by way of an evil path because their roots of unwholesomeness are more numerous and powerful. Therefore, for that evil path as well, from that day onward for eight days, one should perform the rites beginning with the purification of the miserable destinies (*durgatipariśodhana*) according to the procedure taught in the *Durgatipariśodhana-tantra*.
In that regard, as long as the bones have not been brought, one should perform the rite upon a cloth while first uttering the name of the deceased.
Once those bones and the cloth have been brought, one should perform the rites until the eighth day.

There, on the southern side of the dust-mandala, one should prepare a square altar measuring one cubit. Having smeared it with fresh cow-dung, one should sprinkle it thoroughly with products of the cow.

There, having smeared [the ground] and performed the bathing of the mandala with sandalwood, and having adorned it with flowers, one should place upon it a jar endowed with the proper characteristics. It should be provided with sprouts made from the five medicinal herbs, along with *maṇḍūka*, *sūra*, and rice; it should be equipped with a parasol and banners, its neck wrapped in blue cloth, accompanied by the five offerings, well-perfumed, filled with water from sacred fords (*tīrtha*), placed upon a seat made of *darbha* grass, and marked with the insignia of a patriarch.
Then, the practitioner should consecrate it one hundred and eight times with the Yakṣa-mantra joined with the sprinkling-rite, or else with the washing-mantra.

[41*] Then, having drawn an eight-spoked wheel in front of him with white flour—complete with its hub, rim, and flames—and having strewn it with white flowers, he should place a perforated shallow bowl upon an empty jar in the center of that [wheel].
[42*] Thereafter, having circumambulated it clockwise, he should pour [the water] into it without leaving any remainder.
One should perform the three enjoined meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) and bring them into direct perception;
then, reciting the mantras in their proper sequence, one should offer oblations with *siddhārtha* seeds and flowers.
Then one should strike it, or [recite] its name, which is "Pravaraṇa. Now, the mantra words are as follows:

Oṃ, for [Name], the vajra that burns away all sins, hūṃ phaṭ! [46] Oṃ, for [Name], the vajra that purifies all sins, hūṃ phaṭ! [47] Oṃ, reduce to ashes all karmic obscurations of [Name], hūṃ phaṭ! [48] Oṃ bhrūṃ, destroy the obscurations of [Name], hūṃ phaṭ! [49] Oṃ dhrūṃ, purify the obscurations of [Name], hūṃ phaṭ! [50] Oṃ, blaze, blaze! burn, burn! strike, strike! the obscurations of [Name], hūṃ phaṭ!

[51*] Oṃ srūṃ sara 2 prasara 2, [remove] the obstructions of [so-and-so], hūṃ phaṭ! [52*] Oṃ hara 2, [remove] all the obstructions of [so-and-so], hūṃ phaṭ! [53*] Oṃ hūṃ phaṭ, shatter all the obstructions of [so-and-so], hūṃ phaṭ! [54*] Oṃ bhata 2, [remove] all the obstructions of [so-and-so], hūṃ phaṭ! [55*] Oṃ bhraṭa 2, [remove] all the obstructions of [so-and-so], hūṃ phaṭ!

[56*] Oṃ cchinda 2 vidrava 2! May all obscurations of [the person named] so-and-so be destroyed! Hūṃ phaṭ! [57*] Oṃ daha 2! May all causes for the state of rebirth in hell of [the person named] so-and-so be consumed! Hūṃ phaṭ! [58*] Oṃ paca 2! May all causes for the state of rebirth as a hungry ghost (preta) of [the person named] so-and-so be cooked! Hūṃ phaṭ! [59*] Oṃ matha 2! May all causes for the state of rebirth as an animal (tiryak) of [the person named] so-and-so be crushed! Hūṃ phaṭ! [60*] Thus ends the ritual procedure for striking with bones and other substances. [61*] ||
Then, one should wash those bones and so forth with the water from the consecrated vase while reciting the mantra. The mantra is:

*Oṃ namo bhagavate sarvadurgatipariśodhanarājāya tathāgatāyārhate samyaksaṃbuddhāya | tadyathā | Oṃ śodhane 2 viśodhane 2 sarvapāpaviśodhane śuddhe viśuddhe sarvakarmāvaraṇaviśuddhe svāhā.* This is the mantra for washing the bones and so forth. [This is identical to the procedure of Vilāsavajra.]

Then, having cast a flower while reciting the mantra, one should show the path: *mantradhātu...asambhave ratnakiraṇe ratnamālāviśuddhe śodhaya sarvapāpān hūṃ trāṭ*. This is the mantra for showing the way to the destination (*gatisaṃdarśanamantra*). [64*] Having cast the flower into the water, one should purify the path: *oṃ padme 2 padmodbhave sukhāvatyāṃ gacchantu svāhā*. This is the mantra for purifying the path (*mārgaśodhanamantra*).
[65*] In those mantra-words, one should insert the words of exhortation (*codanapada*): "...[it] shall rain down a great rain. [66*]
With a concentrated mind, he should cause auspicious verses (maṅgalagāthā) to be sung from the Geya;
likewise, he should perform this every day at the three junctions of the day or at one junction. Having performed the worship, he should conclude everything according to the prescribed rule.
Therein are the verses of auspiciousness:

May that auspiciousness which belongs to the Buddha—who delights in the welfare of all sentient beings, who is free from faults, whose intellect is purified by the wise, who is beautiful with the armor of the limbs of wisdom, and whose nature is bliss—be yours at this supreme consecration. May that auspiciousness which belongs to the Dharma—which is praised by gods, humans, and asuras, which was taught by him (the Buddha), which is unsurpassed, known throughout the three worlds, and characterized by selflessness—be yours at this supreme consecration.

Whatever auspiciousness belongs to the bearer of the supreme Dharma, who constantly dwells on the true stages, who is the son of the lineage of the Conqueror’s Dharma, who is skillful in benefiting sentient beings, and who is perfectly auspicious—may that auspiciousness be yours at the supreme consecration. These are the verses of auspiciousness; they may be sung as a song even at the time of washing the bones.
Therein is the mantra for dismissal:

[72] *Oṃ, you have accomplished the welfare of all sentient beings; having granted success, go according to your inclination. Go to the realm of the Buddhas, for the sake of returning once more, *mur*.
[73] Then, having performed the *gaṇacakra* at night, one should withdraw everything. [74]
If it is possible, having set in motion the Maṇḍala for Purifying the Evil Destinies according to the ritual procedure, one should perform the rites as prescribed.
Furthermore, the Vajrācārya should [offer] an inheritance; if he too should give it, he should do so in accordance with his wealth.
And he should offer a washed garment to the Ācārya alone.
And it is said:

Whatever is given by one's kinsmen to the preceptor on behalf of the deceased should be understood as being given to him; that is his provision for the journey to heaven. Whatever little is sought after by those desiring Śiva’s favor should be given within seven days.
By that gift, he is honored in the blissful realm of Sukhāvatī.
Whatever funeral rites are performed for whomsoever according to the prescribed ritual,
having performed all those acts, he surely attains the various realms of Sukhāvatī.
Thereafter, having purified those bones and ground them into a fine powder with a stone,
he should cause them to be carried away by a great and vast river with offerings,
or else, having ascended the peak of a great mountain.
By the force of the *parivārtha-saru*, one should scatter that [offering] in that sequence.
Even if, due to the power of extremely cruel karma, he should not go to the blissful and sweet realm of Sukhāvatī— [Note:
The syllable *caṃ* appears in the first line, left margin; it is unclear where this applies.]

Having received the great instruction for the funeral rites from the glorious Bhadrapāda, he would certainly go to the abode of the thirty-three gods, having abandoned the miserable states of existence.
This is the procedure for the funeral rites according to the system of the *Śrī Guhyasamāja*.
[84] This is for the fulfillment of whatever ritual action is not completed from the *Śrī Guhyasamāja*.
Indeed, the ritual action based upon that which is taught in the *Śrīmad-durgatipariśodhana-tantra* has been set forth. O ||
This concludes the *Mṛtasugatiniyojanābhidhāna-maṃtyaṣṭi* (The Eightfold Rite for Directing the Deceased to a Happy Rebirth).
As Ryūgen suggests, it is more likely that this is the composition of the funeral rites (*antyeṣṭi-vidhāna*), [stating]: "This is the work of the venerable scholar Śūnyasamādhivajrapāda. || o ||

In the year 589, on the sixth day of the dark fortnight of Pauṣya, on the day of the moon’s conjunction with the asterism Ārdrā, this was written for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings. May there be auspiciousness for the entire world.
